subject: biology

items.q: Which statement about ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is correct?
items.correct: It is a nucleotide: adenine and ribose joined to a chain of three phosphate groups.
items.misconception: It is a small protein that binds energy released from glucose in respiration.
items.why: Nucleotides are first met as the monomers of nucleic acids, so students file the term under DNA and RNA. ATP is introduced separately in the context of energy and is rarely drawn beside a DNA nucleotide, so the shared structure goes unnoticed. Adenosine triphosphate is a nucleotide: the base adenine, the pentose sugar ribose and three phosphate groups. It is the same adenine nucleotide that is found in RNA, but with three phosphates rather than one, and it is not a protein.
items.specStatementText: ATP carries energy from where it is released to where it is used
items.random_wrong: It is the cell's main long-term reserve of energy, built up like glycogen.

items.q: A cell needs an energy currency that can supply many different reactions in the cytoplasm. Which property makes ATP suitable for this role?
items.correct: It releases energy in an amount suited to a single reaction and is quickly re-formed from ADP.
items.misconception: It holds a very large amount of energy, so that a cell can store it for many weeks between meals.
items.why: ATP is often introduced as 'the energy molecule' or 'energy store' in earlier courses, and the word 'store' suggests something laid down for the future. Students do not meet the turnover figures that show ATP is used within seconds of being made. ATP distributes energy within the cell rather than storing it. Its suitability as an energy currency comes from being rapidly regenerated from ADP and phosphate, so a small pool is used over and over. Reserves of energy are held as glycogen and lipid, which are respired to make ATP when needed.
items.specStatementText: ATP carries energy from where it is released to where it is used
items.random_wrong: It is consumed after one use, so the cell then builds fresh ATP directly from glucose.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes a life process that ATP supplies with energy?
items.correct: Pumping sodium ions out of a neuron against their concentration gradient uses ATP directly.
items.misconception: Water entering a root hair cell by osmosis uses ATP to cross the membrane against its gradient.
items.why: Students learn that active transport needs ATP and over-generalise from the everyday idea that moving anything requires energy. The term 'passive' is not always connected to the idea that no ATP is involved. ATP supplies energy to active transport, which moves substances against their concentration gradient through pumps. Diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis are passive: substances move down their gradients using their own kinetic energy, so no ATP is hydrolysed.
items.specStatementText: What cells spend ATP on
items.random_wrong: Joining amino acids into a polypeptide releases energy, which the cell holds as ATP.

items.q: During a sprint, ATP in muscle fibres is hydrolysed and then re-formed thousands of times. Which statement about the energy transfers is correct?
items.correct: Hydrolysis of ATP releases energy; energy from respiration is needed to re-form it from ADP.
items.misconception: Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate needs an input of energy, and re-forming ATP releases it.
items.why: Students correctly learn that respiration releases energy and that respiration makes ATP, then merge the two so that ATP synthesis itself becomes the energy-releasing step. The direction of the transfer is then reversed. Energy released by oxidizing substrates in respiration is required to synthesize ATP from ADP and phosphate. ATP then releases that energy when it is hydrolysed back to ADP and phosphate at the site where it is needed.
items.specStatementText: Hydrolysing ATP releases energy; making it takes energy in
items.random_wrong: Hydrolysed ATP cannot be re-formed, so each contraction needs new ATP built from a glucose molecule.

items.q: A student writes: 'Cell respiration is when oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it in the lungs.' Which statement correctly evaluates this?
items.correct: It is wrong: this describes gas exchange; cell respiration releases energy from carbon compounds to make ATP inside cells.
items.misconception: It is right: respiration is the exchange of gases at a respiratory surface, which the cells then make use of.
items.why: In everyday English 'respiration' means breathing, and 'respiratory system' names the lungs and airways. The everyday meaning is carried into biology. Cell respiration is a chemical process in every living cell that releases energy from carbon compounds to make ATP. Gas exchange supplies the oxygen used in aerobic respiration and removes the carbon dioxide produced, but it is a separate, physical process of diffusion across a surface.
items.specStatementText: Respiration makes ATP inside cells; gas exchange is something else
items.random_wrong: It is wrong: cell respiration is glucose reacting with oxygen inside cells, and glucose is the only substrate used.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the substrates of cell respiration?
items.correct: Glucose and fatty acids are the main substrates, but many other carbon compounds can be used.
items.misconception: Only glucose can be respired, because it is the reactant in the equation for respiration.
items.why: The word equation for respiration is taught only with glucose, and the mnemonic 'glucose + oxygen' is rehearsed so often that glucose becomes part of the definition of respiration rather than one example of a substrate. Cell respiration releases energy from carbon compounds in general. Glucose and fatty acids are the principal substrates, but many organic compounds can be used; the word equations with glucose are simply the standard examples.
items.specStatementText: Respiration makes ATP inside cells; gas exchange is something else
items.random_wrong: Glucose and fatty acids are the substrates, and either can be used with or without oxygen.

items.q: Which statement about anaerobic cell respiration in humans is correct?
items.correct: Glucose is converted to lactate, and no carbon dioxide is released at all.
items.misconception: Glucose is converted to ethanol and carbon dioxide, as it is in yeast cells.
items.why: The yeast equation (glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide) and the human equation are learned together, and the more memorable yeast products are transferred to humans. In humans, anaerobic respiration converts glucose to lactate with no carbon dioxide released. Ethanol and carbon dioxide are the products of anaerobic respiration in yeast.
items.specStatementText: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans compared
items.random_wrong: Glucose is converted to lactate and carbon dioxide in the cytoplasm of the cell.

items.q: Mature human red blood cells have no mitochondria. Which statement about cell respiration in these cells is correct?
items.correct: They respire anaerobically in the cytoplasm, converting glucose to lactate.
items.misconception: They cannot respire at all, because all cell respiration takes place in mitochondria.
items.why: Mitochondria are labelled 'site of respiration' in cell diagrams from the first year of biology, so students assume every form of respiration is confined to them. Mitochondria are required for aerobic respiration but not for anaerobic respiration. Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm in both cases; in anaerobic respiration the pathway is completed there by conversion of pyruvate to lactate, and the mitochondria are not involved.
items.specStatementText: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans compared
items.random_wrong: They respire anaerobically, and so they gain no ATP from the glucose they take up.

items.q: Aerobic respiration of one glucose molecule yields many times more ATP (roughly 30) than anaerobic respiration (2). Which statement explains the difference?
items.correct: Without oxygen only glycolysis in the cytoplasm yields ATP; with oxygen the mitochondria release far more of the energy in glucose.
items.misconception: Without oxygen the cell uses the little oxygen dissolved in its cytoplasm, so only a small amount of ATP forms.
items.why: Anaerobic respiration is introduced in the context of hard exercise when the body 'cannot get enough oxygen', which suggests a shortage rather than an absence, and the prefix 'an-' is not recognised as meaning 'without'. The difference between the two processes is whether oxygen is required: aerobic respiration requires oxygen, anaerobic respiration does not. Anaerobic respiration proceeds entirely without oxygen: glycolysis and the conversion of pyruvate to lactate both take place in the cytoplasm, so the oxygen-using electron transport chain in the mitochondria is not involved.
items.specStatementText: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans compared
items.random_wrong: Both pathways run in the mitochondria, but without oxygen the mitochondria work more slowly and so make less ATP.

items.q: In a respirometer, carbon dioxide is absorbed by potassium hydroxide. With 5.0 g of germinating seeds, the gas volume in the apparatus fell by 1.2 cm³ in 10 minutes. What is the rate of respiration per gram?
items.correct: 0.024 cm³ of oxygen taken up per gram per minute
items.misconception: 0.024 cm³ of carbon dioxide produced per gram per minute
items.why: Carbon dioxide is the product students expect to detect in respiration experiments (lime water, indicator), so they assume the respirometer detects it too and overlook the role of the alkali. In a respirometer the carbon dioxide produced is absorbed by potassium hydroxide, so it does not contribute to the gas volume. The decrease in volume, shown by the liquid moving towards the tissue, is equal to the volume of oxygen consumed. Without the alkali the volumes would roughly cancel and little movement would be seen.
items.specStatementText: Measuring the rate of respiration
items.random_wrong: 0.12 cm³ of oxygen taken up per gram per minute

items.q: A student measured oxygen uptake by yeast (cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹) at five temperatures: 20 °C 0.10; 30 °C 0.19; 40 °C 0.31; 50 °C 0.26; 60 °C 0.04. Which conclusion is best supported?
items.correct: Rate rises with temperature up to an optimum near 40 °C, then falls as the enzymes of respiration denature.
items.misconception: Rate rises with temperature over the whole range, so the low reading at 60 °C must be an experimental error.
items.why: The kinetic-energy explanation of rates is learned first and is correct over the lower part of the range, so a fall in rate at high temperature is treated as an error rather than as denaturation. Temperature is one of the variables affecting the rate of cell respiration. Because every step is enzyme-catalysed, the rate rises with temperature until the enzymes begin to denature, after which it falls rapidly.
items.specStatementText: Measuring the rate of respiration
items.random_wrong: Above 40 °C the yeast switches to anaerobic respiration, which uses no oxygen, so oxygen uptake falls.

items.q: In one reaction of the Krebs cycle, two hydrogen atoms (each with an electron) are removed from a substrate and accepted by NAD. Which statement describes this reaction?
items.correct: The substrate has been oxidized and NAD has been reduced.
items.misconception: The substrate is reduced and NAD is oxidized by the transfer.
items.why: Students remember that 'something happens to NAD' but attach the wrong label, often because 'reduced' in everyday language means 'made smaller' and gaining hydrogen sounds like an addition. Redox reactions involve both oxidation and reduction. The substrate that loses hydrogen is oxidized; NAD, which accepts the hydrogen, is reduced. Reduced NAD is later oxidized back to NAD when it gives up its electrons.
items.specStatementText: Oxidation is losing hydrogen; NAD carries it
items.random_wrong: Neither substance is oxidized, because no oxygen takes part in it.

items.q: Which statement correctly summarises the stages of glycolysis?
items.correct: Glucose is phosphorylated using ATP, split into two three-carbon molecules that are oxidized, and ATP is then formed.
items.misconception: Glucose is phosphorylated, forming ATP, and then split into two pyruvate molecules that are reduced.
items.why: 'Phosphorylation' is heard most often in the phrase 'phosphorylation of ADP to ATP', so any phosphorylation is assumed to generate ATP. In glycolysis, phosphorylation of glucose is the step that uses ATP, making the hexose more reactive. ATP is formed later, when phosphate groups are transferred from the three-carbon intermediates to ADP.
items.specStatementText: Glycolysis splits glucose into two pyruvate, step by step
items.random_wrong: A single enzyme splits glucose directly into two pyruvate molecules, releasing energy in the form of ATP.

items.q: During glycolysis of one glucose molecule, two ATP are used in phosphorylation and four ATP are formed later. What is the net yield per glucose?
items.correct: A net gain of 2 ATP together with 2 reduced NAD
items.misconception: A net gain of 4 ATP as well as 2 reduced NAD
items.why: The ATP-forming steps are the memorable part of the pathway, and the two ATP used in the first phosphorylation are forgotten when totalling up, so gross yield is reported as net. Glycolysis begins with phosphorylation of glucose using two ATP. Four ATP are formed later, so the net yield is two ATP per glucose, together with two reduced NAD and two pyruvate.
items.specStatementText: Glycolysis splits glucose into two pyruvate, step by step
items.random_wrong: A net gain of 6 ATP plus another 2 reduced NAD

items.q: During intense exercise, muscle cells convert pyruvate to lactate. What is the purpose of this conversion?
items.correct: To regenerate NAD so that glycolysis can continue producing ATP.
items.misconception: To release extra ATP from pyruvate once the mitochondria have stopped working.
items.why: Students know anaerobic respiration 'produces some ATP' and lactate is its named product, so they assume the ATP comes from the lactate-forming step. All of the ATP of anaerobic respiration comes from glycolysis (a net two per glucose). Reducing pyruvate to lactate converts reduced NAD back to NAD, and without this glycolysis would stop for lack of NAD.
items.specStatementText: Making lactate keeps glycolysis running without oxygen
items.random_wrong: To oxidize pyruvate so that more reduced NAD is available to the cell.

items.q: How does anaerobic cell respiration in yeast differ from anaerobic cell respiration in human muscle?
items.correct: Yeast regenerates NAD by turning pyruvate into ethanol and carbon dioxide, not lactate.
items.misconception: Yeast uses a different pathway from glucose to pyruvate, with its own distinct set of enzymes.
items.why: Different end products suggest different processes, and the two are often taught on separate pages with separate equations, so the shared glycolysis is not obvious. The pathways of anaerobic respiration are the same in humans and yeasts apart from the regeneration of NAD using pyruvate. In yeast, pyruvate is decarboxylated and the product is reduced to ethanol; in humans, pyruvate is reduced directly to lactate.
items.specStatementText: Yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide instead
items.random_wrong: Yeast converts pyruvate to ethanol only, since carbon dioxide cannot form without oxygen.

items.q: Yeast is used in baking to make dough rise and in brewing to make beer alcoholic. Which statement explains both uses?
items.correct: Anaerobic respiration of sugars produces carbon dioxide, which raises the dough, and ethanol, which remains in the beer.
items.misconception: The carbon dioxide that raises dough comes from aerobic respiration, since anaerobic respiration releases none.
items.why: Having learned that human anaerobic respiration produces no carbon dioxide, and believing that carbon dioxide forms when oxygen is used, students generalise to all anaerobic respiration. Carbon dioxide in respiration comes from decarboxylation, not from oxygen. Yeast decarboxylates pyruvate in anaerobic respiration, releasing carbon dioxide; this is why yeast makes bread dough rise and carbonates beer.
items.specStatementText: Yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide instead
items.random_wrong: Yeast produces lactate, as human muscle does, which sours the dough and makes the beer alcoholic.

items.q: What happens to pyruvate in the link reaction of aerobic cell respiration?
items.correct: It is oxidized and decarboxylated to a 2C acetyl group, which coenzyme A carries to the Krebs cycle.
items.misconception: It enters the Krebs cycle directly, where it combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate.
items.why: Summaries of respiration list 'glycolysis, Krebs cycle, electron transport chain', and the link reaction is easily dropped because it is short and has no memorable name. The link reaction converts pyruvate (3C) to an acetyl group (2C), releasing carbon dioxide and reducing NAD. The acetyl group is transferred by coenzyme A to the Krebs cycle, where it joins oxaloacetate (4C) to form citrate (6C).
items.specStatementText: The link reaction turns pyruvate into a 2C acetyl group
items.random_wrong: It reacts with oxygen in the matrix, forming carbon dioxide and a two-carbon acetyl group that enters the cycle.

items.q: Which statement about the Krebs cycle is correct?
items.correct: Citrate (6C) forms when an acetyl group (2C) joins oxaloacetate (4C), which is then regenerated.
items.misconception: Oxaloacetate is used up in each turn of the cycle, so it must be supplied continually from pyruvate.
items.why: In the linear pathways of glycolysis and the link reaction every reactant is consumed, and students carry that expectation into the cycle without noticing that a cycle returns to its starting compound. Citrate is produced by transfer of an acetyl group to oxaloacetate, and oxaloacetate is regenerated by the reactions of the Krebs cycle, including four oxidations and two decarboxylations. Only the two carbons of the acetyl group are new input each turn.
items.specStatementText: The Krebs cycle oxidizes acetyl groups and regenerates oxaloacetate
items.random_wrong: Most of the ATP from aerobic respiration is formed directly by the reactions of the cycle itself.

items.q: One acetyl group enters the Krebs cycle and oxaloacetate is regenerated. Which account of one turn of the cycle is correct?
items.correct: Two decarboxylations give off carbon dioxide, four dehydrogenations reduce carriers, one ATP forms.
items.misconception: Two carbon dioxide molecules form when oxygen oxidizes the carbon atoms of the acetyl group directly.
items.why: The Krebs cycle is labelled 'aerobic', it takes place in the mitochondrion where oxygen is used, and it releases carbon dioxide, so students assume oxygen must react there to form the carbon dioxide. The oxidations in the Krebs cycle are dehydrogenation reactions: hydrogen is removed to reduce NAD. Carbon dioxide comes from decarboxylation. The cycle depends on oxygen only indirectly, because NAD is regenerated when the electron transport chain passes electrons to oxygen.
items.specStatementText: The Krebs cycle oxidizes acetyl groups and regenerates oxaloacetate
items.random_wrong: Each of the four oxidations forms one ATP directly, so the cycle yields most of the cell's ATP supply.

items.q: What is the role of reduced NAD in aerobic cell respiration?
items.correct: It passes a pair of electrons to the first carrier of the electron transport chain, becoming NAD again.
items.misconception: It phosphorylates ADP directly in the matrix, so each reduced NAD becomes a fixed number of ATP.
items.why: Yield tables that convert reduced NAD into 'ATP equivalents' make it look as if reduced NAD is directly exchanged for ATP, and the intervening chain and gradient are skipped. Energy is transferred when reduced NAD passes a pair of electrons to the first carrier in the chain, converting reduced NAD back to NAD. The chain generates a proton gradient, and ATP synthase couples the flow of protons to phosphorylation of ADP.
items.specStatementText: Reduced NAD hands its electrons to the chain
items.random_wrong: It carries hydrogen from the Krebs cycle only, because glycolysis in the cytoplasm forms none.

items.q: Isolated mitochondria are supplied with pyruvate and oxygen. A poison then blocks the first carrier of the electron transport chain, and the Krebs cycle also stops. Which statement explains why the cycle stops?
items.correct: Reduced NAD can no longer pass its electrons to the chain, so no NAD is regenerated for the cycle's oxidations.
items.misconception: The poison prevents oxygen from reaching the matrix, so the cycle can no longer oxidize citrate to oxaloacetate.
items.why: The Krebs cycle is labelled 'aerobic', it takes place in the mitochondrion where oxygen is used, and it releases carbon dioxide, so students assume oxygen must react there to form the carbon dioxide. The oxidations in the Krebs cycle are dehydrogenation reactions: hydrogen is removed to reduce NAD. Carbon dioxide comes from decarboxylation. The cycle depends on oxygen only indirectly, because NAD is regenerated when the electron transport chain passes electrons to oxygen.
items.specStatementText: Reduced NAD hands its electrons to the chain
items.random_wrong: Reduced NAD can no longer phosphorylate ADP directly, and the cycle runs on the ATP that this provides.

items.q: How is the proton gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane generated?
items.correct: Energy released as electrons flow along the chain pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space.
items.misconception: Protons are pumped from the intermembrane space into the matrix as electrons flow along the chain of carriers.
items.why: Students know ATP is made in the matrix and associate the protons with ATP synthesis, so they place the accumulation of protons where the ATP ends up. The flow of electrons along the chain releases energy used to pump protons from the matrix across the inner membrane into the intermembrane space. Protons then flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase, driving ATP synthesis on the matrix side.
items.specStatementText: Electron flow pumps protons across the inner membrane
items.random_wrong: Hydrolysis of ATP supplies the energy needed to pump protons across the inner membrane into the intermembrane space.

items.q: How does ATP synthase couple the proton gradient to the synthesis of ATP?
items.correct: Protons flow through it down their gradient into the matrix, releasing energy that phosphorylates ADP.
items.misconception: It hydrolyses ATP to pump protons across the inner membrane into the intermembrane space, building the gradient.
items.why: ATP synthase is drawn as a large membrane protein next to the carriers that pump protons, and its name links it to ATP, so it is assumed to be another pump. ATP synthase couples release of energy from the proton gradient with phosphorylation of ADP. Protons diffuse through it from the intermembrane space into the matrix, and the energy released as they move down the gradient is used to join phosphate to ADP.
items.specStatementText: Protons flow back through ATP synthase, making ATP
items.random_wrong: Water moves through it by osmosis into the matrix, and the resulting pressure change forces phosphate onto ADP.

items.q: A chemical makes the inner mitochondrial membrane freely permeable to protons. Electron flow and oxygen consumption continue, but ATP synthesis stops. Which statement explains these observations?
items.correct: Protons leak back into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase, so no gradient remains to drive ADP phosphorylation.
items.misconception: Electrons leak through the membrane instead of reaching oxygen, so no energy arrives at ATP synthase.
items.why: 'Electron transport' and 'proton pumping' are both taught for the same membrane, and diagrams with many arrows make it easy to mix up which particle crosses the membrane. Electrons flow along the electron transport chain from carrier to carrier. The energy released is used to pump protons from the matrix to the intermembrane space, generating a proton gradient. It is protons, not electrons, that flow back through ATP synthase.
items.specStatementText: Protons flow back through ATP synthase, making ATP
items.random_wrong: Water enters the matrix by osmosis, diluting the ADP and phosphate so that they can no longer be joined together.

items.q: What is the role of oxygen in aerobic cell respiration?
items.correct: It accepts electrons from the final carrier of the chain and protons from the matrix, forming water.
items.misconception: It combines with carbon atoms from the acetyl group in the Krebs cycle to form the carbon dioxide released.
items.why: The overall equation shows oxygen going in and carbon dioxide coming out, and combustion in chemistry joins carbon to oxygen, so the carbon dioxide is assumed to be made from the oxygen. The oxygen consumed in aerobic respiration becomes water: it is the terminal electron acceptor at the end of the electron transport chain. The carbon dioxide released comes from decarboxylation in the link reaction and the Krebs cycle.
items.specStatementText: Oxygen takes the electrons at the end of the chain
items.random_wrong: It is not needed for the chain to run; it is used only in the last step to form water.

items.q: A student claims: 'Without oxygen the electron transport chain keeps running; only the formation of water stops.' Which statement correctly evaluates this claim?
items.correct: Incorrect: with no terminal acceptor the final carrier remains reduced and electron flow stops.
items.misconception: Correct: the chain needs only reduced NAD to keep running, and oxygen is required just to make water.
items.why: Oxygen appears at the end of every diagram of the chain, producing water, so its role looks like a minor finishing step rather than the condition for any flow at all. Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor. It accepts electrons from the chain and protons from the matrix, producing water and allowing continued flow of electrons along the chain. Without it every carrier becomes reduced and electron flow, proton pumping and ATP synthesis by chemiosmosis all stop.
items.specStatementText: Oxygen takes the electrons at the end of the chain
items.random_wrong: Incorrect: the chain stops because the Krebs cycle needs oxygen to keep supplying it with reduced NAD.

items.q: Which statement correctly compares lipids and carbohydrates as respiratory substrates?
items.correct: Lipids yield more energy per gram, as they have less oxygen and more oxidizable hydrogen.
items.misconception: Carbohydrates yield more energy per gram, because they are the body's main and most readily used fuel.
items.why: Carbohydrate is presented as the main respiratory substrate and 'quick energy' food, so students infer it must be the richer fuel; the distinction between how readily a substrate is used and how much energy it contains is not made. Lipids yield more energy per gram than carbohydrates. A fatty acid has less oxygen and more hydrogen and carbon that can be oxidized, so more reduced NAD is formed per gram and more ATP is produced by chemiosmosis.
items.specStatementText: Lipids give more energy per gram but need oxygen
items.random_wrong: Lipids yield more energy per gram, because they contain more oxygen atoms that can be oxidized.

items.q: A sprinter's leg muscles rely on anaerobic respiration during a 100 m race. Which statement explains why the muscles cannot use fatty acids to supply this energy?
items.correct: Fatty acids enter aerobic respiration as acetyl-CoA and cannot enter glycolysis, the only stage that yields ATP without oxygen.
items.misconception: Fatty acids must first be converted into glucose, and this conversion is far too slow to keep pace with a sprint.
items.why: Glycolysis is the only entry point students learn in detail, so every substrate is assumed to be converted into glucose to use it. The two-carbon acetyl groups from the breakdown of fatty acids enter the pathway via acetyl-CoA, bypassing glycolysis. Because glycolysis and anaerobic respiration occur only if carbohydrate is the substrate, fatty acids can be respired only aerobically.
items.specStatementText: Lipids give more energy per gram but need oxygen
items.random_wrong: Fatty acids can be respired anaerobically, but the muscle prefers glucose because it is much faster to break down.

items.q: What happens to ATP after it has supplied energy to a process?
items.correct: It becomes ADP and phosphate, which are rejoined to make ATP again using energy from cell respiration; ATP is recycled, not destroyed.
items.misconception: Once ATP has been used it is broken down and lost, so the cell must make fresh ATP from scratch out of glucose every time it needs energy.
items.why: The word 'used' suggests consumption, and respiration is taught as 'making ATP from glucose', so students picture glucose as the raw material for each ATP molecule rather than ADP and phosphate. The cycle between ATP and ADP is often shown only once. Hydrolysis of ATP gives ADP and phosphate, and the same ADP and phosphate are recombined to form ATP using energy released in respiration. The energy comes from glucose; the ADP does not. A cell recycles each ADP molecule many times a day.
items.specStatementText: Hydrolysing ATP releases energy; making it takes energy in
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do cell processes such as muscle contraction use energy directly from glucose?
items.correct: No. Energy is released from glucose in respiration and used to make ATP; it is hydrolysis of ATP that supplies energy directly to the process.
items.misconception: Glucose is the cell's fuel, so processes like contraction or active transport get their energy straight from breaking glucose down, and ATP is a minor by-product.
items.why: Earlier courses summarise respiration as 'glucose releases energy for the cell' without mentioning ATP, so glucose is remembered as the direct energy source. ATP is added later and can seem like an unnecessary extra step. ATP is the molecule that distributes energy within cells. Energy released from glucose (or other carbon compounds) is transferred to ATP by respiration, and ATP hydrolysis then supplies energy to active transport, anabolism and movement. Processes do not draw energy from glucose directly.
items.specStatementText: ATP carries energy from where it is released to where it is used
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does building a polypeptide from amino acids release energy or require it?
items.correct: It requires energy: anabolic reactions, which synthesize macromolecules, are supplied with energy by ATP.
items.misconception: Joining molecules together releases energy, because reactions that form bonds are the ones that give out energy, and only breaking down food releases energy in respiration.
items.why: Students hear that energy is released when bonds form in chemistry and confuse this with the overall energy change of a biosynthetic reaction. They also pair 'anabolism' with 'catabolism' without securely attaching 'requires energy' to the right term. Anabolism is the synthesis of larger molecules from smaller ones, and it requires an input of energy that ATP supplies. Catabolic reactions such as respiration release energy. Protein synthesis, DNA replication and polysaccharide synthesis are all ATP-consuming processes.

items.q: Does moving chromosomes to the poles of a cell during mitosis use ATP?
items.correct: Yes. Movement of cell components such as chromosomes, and of whole cells, is driven by motor proteins that hydrolyse ATP.
items.misconception: Chromosomes are pulled apart passively as the spindle fibres shorten, like a stretched elastic band relaxing, so no ATP is needed.
items.why: Diagrams of mitosis show spindle fibres 'contracting' to pull chromosomes, and nothing in the drawing hints at an energy input, so the movement looks mechanical and free. Movement of the whole cell or of cell components such as chromosomes is one of the life processes that ATP supplies with energy. Motor proteins (kinesins and dynein) that move chromosomes along the spindle use energy from ATP hydrolysis.
items.specStatementText: What cells spend ATP on
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does cell respiration make energy?
items.correct: No. Energy cannot be created. Respiration releases energy that is already stored in the bonds of carbon compounds and transfers it to ATP.
items.misconception: Respiration produces or creates energy for the cell; the cell would have no energy without it.
items.why: Everyday phrases such as 'energy production' and 'mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell' suggest energy is manufactured. The distinction between releasing stored chemical energy and creating energy is not made explicit. Cell respiration is a system for producing ATP using energy released from carbon compounds. The energy already exists in the substrate; respiration transfers it to ATP in a controlled series of reactions, with some lost as heat.
items.specStatementText: Respiration makes ATP inside cells; gas exchange is something else
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does anaerobic respiration in humans produce any ATP?
items.correct: Yes, a small amount: a net two ATP per glucose from glycolysis, compared with many times more from aerobic respiration.
items.misconception: Anaerobic respiration produces no ATP at all; it just makes lactate while the cell waits for oxygen.
items.why: Anaerobic respiration is presented as a 'poor' or 'emergency' pathway with lactate as its product, and the small ATP yield is easily rounded down to nothing. The two types of respiration differ in their relative yields of ATP: anaerobic respiration yields a net two ATP per glucose, from glycolysis alone, while aerobic respiration yields far more. The small yield is why the pathway is used only when oxygen is insufficient.
items.specStatementText: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans compared
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can fatty acids be used as a substrate for anaerobic respiration?
items.correct: No. Only carbohydrate can be respired anaerobically; fatty acids are respired only aerobically.
items.misconception: Any respiratory substrate, including fats, can be used either with or without oxygen, since respiration is respiration.
items.why: Substrates and oxygen requirement are taught as separate lists, so students do not connect the choice of substrate with whether oxygen is available. Anaerobic respiration in humans uses glucose (carbohydrate) only. Fatty acids can be used as substrates only in aerobic respiration, which is one of the differences between the two processes.
items.specStatementText: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans compared

items.q: Is carbon dioxide produced in anaerobic respiration in humans?
items.correct: No. The only product is lactate; carbon dioxide is produced in aerobic respiration, and in anaerobic respiration in yeast, but not in human anaerobic respiration.
items.misconception: All respiration gives off carbon dioxide, so anaerobic respiration in muscle produces carbon dioxide as well as lactate.
items.why: Carbon dioxide is the product that students test for in school practical work on respiration, and it appears in both the aerobic and the yeast equations, so it is generalised to every type of respiration. The types of waste product differ between aerobic and anaerobic respiration. Aerobic respiration in humans produces carbon dioxide and water; anaerobic respiration produces only lactate: glucose → lactate.
items.specStatementText: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans compared

items.q: What is the rate of respiration if 1.2 cm³ of oxygen is used by 5.0 g of tissue in 10 minutes?
items.correct: 0.024 cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹: divide the volume by the time (1.2 / 10 = 0.12 cm³ min⁻¹) and by the mass (0.12 / 5.0 = 0.024).
items.misconception: The rate is the total volume change that was measured, or the change per minute without allowing for the mass of tissue.
items.why: Students record the volume change as the result of the experiment and report it directly. Dividing by time is remembered, but dividing by mass to allow comparison between samples is often left out because it was not part of GCSE rate calculations. The rate of cell respiration is a change in volume of gas per unit time, and is expressed per unit mass so that samples of different size can be compared. Both divisions are needed: volume ÷ time ÷ mass.

items.q: Do germinating seeds take up oxygen?
items.correct: Yes. Germinating seeds respire aerobically, taking up oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide; they do not photosynthesize.
items.misconception: Plant material gives off oxygen because plants photosynthesize, so seeds in a respirometer release oxygen rather than absorbing it.
items.why: Plants are taught as the organisms that produce oxygen, and respiration in plants receives little attention before IB, so any plant material is assumed to release oxygen. All living cells respire, including plant cells. Germinating seeds have no chlorophyll and are respiring rapidly, so in a respirometer they consume oxygen and the gas volume decreases.

items.q: If oxygen uptake by yeast falls at high temperature, has the yeast switched to anaerobic respiration?
items.correct: No. A fall in oxygen uptake at high temperature is due to denaturation of the enzymes of respiration; anaerobic respiration is a response to lack of oxygen, not to heat.
items.misconception: Whenever oxygen uptake falls, the organism must have switched to anaerobic respiration.
items.why: 'Switching to anaerobic respiration' is the explanation students learn for reduced oxygen use during exercise, and it becomes a general-purpose answer for any decrease in oxygen consumption. Cells respire anaerobically when oxygen is unavailable or insufficient. When oxygen is freely available and the rate falls with rising temperature, the cause is denaturation of enzymes, which slows every stage of respiration.

items.q: Can a substrate be oxidized in a reaction in which no oxygen takes part?
items.correct: Yes. Oxidation is loss of electrons; removal of hydrogen (with its electron) from a substrate oxidizes it, whether or not oxygen is present.
items.misconception: Oxidation means adding oxygen, so a reaction with no oxygen in it cannot be an oxidation.
items.why: Oxidation is first defined as 'gain of oxygen' in early chemistry, and the name of the process reinforces that definition. The electron-based definition is met later and does not displace it. In cell respiration, oxidation is a process of electron loss. When hydrogen with an electron is removed from a substrate (dehydrogenation), the substrate has been oxidized even though no oxygen is involved. This is how glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle oxidize substrates.
items.specStatementText: Oxidation is losing hydrogen; NAD carries it
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When a substrate is dehydrogenated, does the hydrogen carrier change?
items.correct: Yes. Oxidation and reduction always occur together: the substrate is oxidized and the carrier (NAD) is reduced.
items.misconception: Only the substrate changes in a dehydrogenation; the carrier just holds the hydrogen for a while and is not chemically altered.
items.why: Carriers are described as 'carrying' or 'holding' hydrogen, which sounds like a passive container rather than a molecule taking part in a redox reaction. A redox reaction involves both oxidation and reduction. When a substrate is oxidized by removal of hydrogen, NAD is reduced by accepting it; the two changes are inseparable.
items.specStatementText: Oxidation is losing hydrogen; NAD carries it
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is glycolysis a single reaction?
items.correct: No. It is a stepwise pathway of about ten reactions, each catalysed by a different enzyme.
items.misconception: One enzyme splits glucose into two pyruvate molecules in a single step.
items.why: Glycolysis is summarised as 'glucose → 2 pyruvate', and the intermediates are not required, so the summary is mistaken for the mechanism. Glucose is converted to pyruvate by stepwise reactions: phosphorylation, lysis, oxidation and ATP formation. Each step in the pathway is catalysed by a different enzyme, even though the names of the intermediates are not required.
items.specStatementText: Glycolysis splits glucose into two pyruvate, step by step
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is pyruvate oxidized or reduced when it is converted to lactate?
items.correct: Reduced: pyruvate accepts hydrogen from reduced NAD, which is thereby oxidized back to NAD.
items.misconception: Pyruvate is oxidized to lactate, producing more reduced NAD for the cell.
items.why: Respiration is described throughout as oxidizing substrates, so every step is assumed to be an oxidation, and the reversal needed to recycle NAD is overlooked. In anaerobic respiration, reduced NAD passes its hydrogen to pyruvate, forming lactate. Pyruvate is reduced and reduced NAD is oxidized to NAD, which returns to glycolysis.
items.specStatementText: Making lactate keeps glycolysis running without oxygen
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do yeast cells produce lactate in anaerobic respiration?
items.correct: No. Yeast converts pyruvate to ethanol and carbon dioxide; lactate is the product in humans.
items.misconception: Anaerobic respiration is the same in all organisms, so yeast produces lactate just as human muscle does.
items.why: Anaerobic respiration is met first in the context of human exercise, and the lactate equation is learned as 'the' anaerobic equation, so it is applied to every organism. The pathways of anaerobic respiration are the same in humans and yeasts as far as pyruvate. They differ in how NAD is regenerated and therefore in the final products: lactate in humans, ethanol and carbon dioxide in yeast.
items.specStatementText: Yeast makes ethanol and carbon dioxide instead
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is coenzyme A an enzyme?
items.correct: No. Coenzyme A is a carrier molecule that accepts an acetyl group and transfers it to the Krebs cycle; it is not a catalyst.
items.misconception: Coenzyme A is the enzyme that catalyses the link reaction or the formation of citrate.
items.why: The name contains 'enzyme', and it appears in the same sentence as the reactions it is involved in, so it is read as the catalyst. Coenzyme A binds the two-carbon acetyl group formed in the link reaction (or from fatty acid breakdown), forming acetyl-CoA. It hands the acetyl group to oxaloacetate and is released unchanged to be reused; the reactions themselves are catalysed by enzymes.
items.specStatementText: The link reaction turns pyruvate into a 2C acetyl group

items.q: Is most of the ATP of aerobic respiration made directly in the Krebs cycle?
items.correct: No. The Krebs cycle forms only one ATP per turn; most ATP is made by chemiosmosis, using the reduced NAD that the cycle produces.
items.misconception: The Krebs cycle is the main energy-releasing stage, so it produces most of the cell's ATP directly.
items.why: The Krebs cycle is where the substrate is fully oxidized to carbon dioxide, so it feels like the place where the energy is 'taken out'. The role of reduced NAD as the carrier of most of that energy is not appreciated. The yield of the Krebs cycle is a small amount of ATP and a large amount of reduced NAD. The energy in reduced NAD is transferred to the electron transport chain, and most ATP is made by ATP synthase using the proton gradient.
items.specStatementText: The Krebs cycle oxidizes acetyl groups and regenerates oxaloacetate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where does the reduced NAD used by the electron transport chain come from?
items.correct: From glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle.
items.misconception: All reduced NAD comes from the Krebs cycle, because that is the stage inside the mitochondrion.
items.why: The Krebs cycle produces the most reduced NAD and is taught immediately before the chain, so the reduced NAD from glycolysis in the cytoplasm and from the link reaction is forgotten. Reduced NAD comes from glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle. All of it passes electrons to the electron transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
items.specStatementText: Reduced NAD hands its electrons to the chain
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What supplies the energy for pumping protons into the intermembrane space?
items.correct: Energy released as electrons pass along the carriers of the electron transport chain.
items.misconception: The proton pumps are active transport, so they must be powered by hydrolysis of ATP.
items.why: Active transport is defined as 'using ATP', so any pumping against a gradient is assumed to hydrolyse ATP, even in the process that makes ATP. The generation of the proton gradient is driven by the flow of electrons along the electron transport chain: energy released at each transfer is used to move protons across the membrane. This is the process that makes ATP, not one that uses it.
items.specStatementText: Electron flow pumps protons across the inner membrane
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is chemiosmosis the osmosis of water across the mitochondrial membrane?
items.correct: No. Chemiosmosis is the diffusion of protons down a concentration gradient across a membrane, coupled to ATP synthesis; water is not involved.
items.misconception: Chemiosmosis is a type of osmosis, so water moves across the inner membrane and this drives ATP production.
items.why: The word contains 'osmosis', which students know as movement of water, so they assume water is what moves. Chemiosmosis is the movement of protons (hydrogen ions) across a membrane down their concentration gradient through ATP synthase, releasing energy that is used to synthesize ATP. The name reflects a chemical gradient, not water movement.
items.specStatementText: Protons flow back through ATP synthase, making ATP
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where is ATP made by ATP synthase: in the matrix or in the intermembrane space?
items.correct: In the matrix. Protons flow from the intermembrane space through ATP synthase into the matrix, and ADP is phosphorylated on the matrix side.
items.misconception: ATP is made in the intermembrane space, because that is where the protons build up.
items.why: Students place ATP synthesis wherever the protons accumulate, without following the protons through the enzyme to the other side. Protons accumulate in the intermembrane space and flow down their gradient through ATP synthase into the matrix. ATP synthase phosphorylates ADP as they pass, so ATP is released into the matrix.
items.specStatementText: Protons flow back through ATP synthase, making ATP
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why do lipids release more energy per gram than carbohydrates?
items.correct: Because they contain less oxygen and more hydrogen and carbon that can be oxidized; the hydrogen removed reduces NAD, which drives ATP synthesis.
items.misconception: Lipids contain more oxygen than carbohydrates, so more of the molecule can be oxidized to release energy.
items.why: Students link 'oxidation' with 'oxygen' and reason that a molecule richer in oxygen has more to offer; they have not connected energy yield with the hydrogen removed by dehydrogenation. Oxidation in respiration is removal of hydrogen. Carbohydrates are already partly oxidized (one oxygen per carbon); fatty acids have far less oxygen and more hydrogen per carbon, so more hydrogen can be removed to reduce NAD and more ATP is made per gram.
items.specStatementText: Lipids give more energy per gram but need oxygen
